'''''Sphaeropteris medullaris''''',  [[Synonym (taxonomy)|synonym]] '''''Cyathea medullaris''''',<ref name=CFLW/> commonly known as '''mamaku''' or '''black tree fern''', is a large [[tree fern]] up to {{cvt|20|m}} tall with a trunk up to 20 cm [[diameter at breast height]].{{sfn|Large|Braggins|2004|p=222}} It is distributed across the south-west Pacific from [[Fiji]] to [[Pitcairn Islands|Pitcairn Island]] and is a common plant found in forests of New Zealand.

==Description==
[[File:Cyathea medullaris Sw.jpg|thumb|left|Illustration of ''Sphaeropteris medullaris'' by [[William Jackson Hooker]] (1862)]]
The trunk is black and covered with distinctive hexagonal [[Stipe (botany)|stipe]] bases. The [[frond]]s may be up to {{cvt|6|m}} long, and arch upwards from the crown.<ref name="MeaningTrees"/> Occasionally they can be {{cvt|7|m}} in length with [[Petiole (botany)|petioles]] up to {{cvt|9|cm}} thick.<ref> New Zealand Journal of Botany, Volume 17 issue 1 (March 1979) page  100 (Table 1)</ref> Dead fronds are shed except in very young plants. The primary [[pinnation|pinnae]] are from {{cvt|40|cm}} to {{cvt|1|m}} long, and the undersides have scales with spines along their margins. As many as 40,000 leaflets have been counted on a single frond.<ref>{{cite book | last1= Crookes | first1= Marguerite M.A. | last2= Dobbie | first2= H. B. | date= 1973|edition=6th | title= New Zealand Ferns | location= Christchurch | publisher= Whitcomb & Tombs | page= 134 }}</ref> The stipes are thick, black, very rough to the touch, and are similarly covered in black scales with marginal spines. ''Sphaeropteris medullaris'' can be readily distinguished from related species by the hexagonal stipe scars on the trunk, and by the scales with spines on their margins.<ref name="NZPCN">{{cite web |title=''Cyathea medullaris'' |work=New Zealand Plant Conservation Network |url=http://www.nzpcn.org.nz/flora_details.asp?ID=2097 |access-date=2010-10-04}}</ref><ref name="TIPU">{{cite web |title=''Cyathea medullaris'' (G.Forst.) Sw. (1801) |work=Ngā Tipu o Aotearoa — New Zealand Plants |url=http://nzflora.landcareresearch.co.nz/default.aspx?selected=NameDetails&TabNum=0&NameId=ED1E8156-2513-4F9A-BC87-A863C93A57E8 |access-date=2008-05-02}}</ref> Fully grown trees can reach a height of {{cvt|20|m}}, making the species the tallest tree fern found in New Zealand.<ref name="MeaningTrees"/> ''Sphaeropteris medullaris'' is one of the fastest growing tree ferns alongside ''[[Sphaeropteris excelsa]]'', with both species growing as much as {{cvt|50|cm}} a year.{{sfn|Large|Braggins|2004|p=19}}

The tree produces a red [[mucilage]] when the trunk is cut, which is a [[non-Newtonian fluid]].<ref name="MeaningTrees"/>

==Taxonomy and etymology==
The species was first described by German botanist [[Johann Jakob Bernhardi]] in 1801 as ''Sphaeropteris medullaris''.<ref>{{cite Q|Q134533781}}</ref> The species epithet ''medullaris'' means [[pith]]y, referring to the white, edible substance found on the inside of the tree fern's trunk.<ref name="MeaningTrees">{{cite q|Q118646408|pp=90-93}}</ref> Sources variously refer to the species as ''Sphaeropteris medullaris'' or ''Cyathea medullaris''. ''[[Sphaeropteris]]'' is a [[clade]] within the family [[Cyatheaceae]]. While some sources prefer a broader definition of the genus ''[[Cyathea]]'' and treats ''Sphaeropteris'' as a sub-genus, the [[Pteridophyte Phylogeny Group]] classification of 2016 (PPG I) treats ''Sphaeropteris'' as a genus separate to ''Cyathea''.<ref name=PPGI>{{citation |author=PPG I |year=2016 |title=A community-derived classification for extant lycophytes and ferns |journal=Journal of Systematics and Evolution |volume=54 |issue=6 |pages=563–603 |doi=10.1111/jse.12229|s2cid=39980610 |doi-access=free }}</ref>

The species is referred to as mamaku or mamau in several [[Polynesian languages]], including [[Māori language|Māori]]. Early European settlers to New Zealand referred to the species as black tree fern, or as black mamaku.<ref name="MeaningTrees"/> Other [[Māori language|Māori]] names include katātā, kōrau, and pītau.

==Distribution==
The species is found across many southwestern [[Pacific Ocean]] islands, including [[New Zealand]], [[Fiji]], the [[Marquesas Islands]], [[Tahiti]], the [[Austral Islands]], and [[Pitcairn Islands|Pitcairn Island]]. It is not present in the [[Kermadec Islands]].<ref name="MeaningTrees"/>{{sfn|Large|Braggins|2004|p=222}}

''Sphaeropteris medullaris'' is common in lowland forest throughout the [[North Island]] of New Zealand. In the [[South Island]], its distribution is more localised. It is fairly common in wetter coastal areas, but rare in the drier eastern parts and absent in [[Canterbury, New Zealand|Canterbury]] and [[Otago]]. In New Zealand it also occurs on the [[Three Kings Islands]] in the far north, on [[Stewart Island / Rakiura]] in the far south and in the [[Chatham Islands]].<ref>{{cite book |first1=P.J. |last1=Brownsey |first2=J.C. |last2=Smith-Dodsworth |date=1989 |title=New Zealand Ferns and Allied Plants |publisher=David Bateman Ltd |page=87 |isbn=1-86953-003-9}}</ref>

==Ecology==
[[File:Tree ferns on valley slope.jpg|thumb|''Sphaeropteris medullaris'' can colonise areas of disturbed forests]]

''Sphaeropteris medullaris'' is a coloniser of disturbed hillside areas in many high humidity forests of New Zealand, a role taken by [[mānuka]] and [[Kunzea ericoides|kānuka]] in many areas of New Zealand. It is likely that mānuka and kānuka only recently became more likely to establish disturbed soil, since the arrival of people to New Zealand, and the impact of fires on native forests.<ref name="MeaningTrees"/> C. medularis is one of the few ferns which sometimes forms pure stands excluding almost all other vegetation.{{sfn|Large|Braggins|2004|p=222}} They can grow 50 cm a year "or more".{{sfn|Large|Braggins|2004|p=222}}

==Cultivation==
''Sphaeropteris medullaris'' will grow from fresh spores, but this is slow. Plants are easy to transplant when they are young. It is also possible to plant newly felled trunks which will generally sprout again, provided they are watered with care. They are hardy in various conditions once established.<ref name="NZPCN"/><ref name="TIPU"/> It has gained the [[Royal Horticultural Society]]'s [[Award of Garden Merit]] as an ornamental.<ref>{{cite web |title=AGM Plants July 2021 © RHS – ORNAMENTAL |url=https://www.rhs.org.uk/plants/pdfs/agm-lists/agm-ornamentals.pdf |publisher=The Royal Horticultural Society |accessdate=21 December 2021}}</ref>

==Uses and traditional culture==
In traditional [[Māori culture]], the drooping fronds of ''Sphaeropteris medullaris'' is associated with grief and sorrow. Traditional stories describe Mamaku and [[Southern royal albatross|Toroa]] (the albatross) as human lovers who would argue and bicker. Their arguing angered the gods, who turned Toroa into an albatross, and Mamaku into a tree fern.<ref name="MeaningTrees"/>

The 1889 book ''The Useful Native Plants of Australia'' records that Indigenous Australians ate the pith of this fern tree which contained a certain amount of starch similar to sago.<ref>{{cite book |author=J. H. Maiden |year=1889 |title=The useful native plants of Australia : Including Tasmania |publisher=Turner and Henderson, Sydney |url=https://primo-slnsw.hosted.exlibrisgroup.com/primo-explore/fulldisplay?docid=SLNSW_ALMA21105097830002626&context=L&vid=SLNSW&search_scope=EEA&tab=default_tab&lang=en_US}}</ref> The plant is also a traditional food source in New Zealand, where both the pith and coiled fern fronds are used.<ref name="MeaningTrees"/> Traditionally, ''Sphaeropteris medullaris'' was seen as a food for difficult times, as harvesting the pith will typically kill the tree.<ref name="MeaningTrees"/> The internal part of ''S. medullaris''<nowiki/>' trunk, which has a malleable and viscous texture, was steamed for consumption and eaten when cold.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Fuller |first=David |title=Maori Food and Cookery |publisher=A.H. & A.W. Reed |year=1978 |isbn=0589049763 |pages=7}}</ref> The bark is used to create a [[taonga pūoro]] (traditional Māori instrument) called rōria.<ref name="MeaningTrees"/>

Tree fern trunks, including those of ''S. medullaris'', have been used as rough building material and also for makeshift trackwork.<ref name="TIPU"/>
